paper.title_en: 3D Hydrodynamic Simulations of Micro-Tidal Disruption Events Favor a Narrow, Ultra-relativistic Jet for GRB250702B
paper.abstract_en: The longest detected $γ$-ray burst, GRB250702B, exhibited seven hours of prompt $γ$-ray emission, a day-long X-ray precursor, and a weeks-long fading X-ray tail. We show that a jetted micro-TDE can explain this unusual evolution by satisfying tight constraints imposed on the engine by the requirements of jet stability and observed energetics. Using 3D hydrodynamic AREPO simulations of a $1M_\odot$ star disrupted by a $10M_\odot$ black hole, we find that within several hours the debris forms a quasi-steady envelope, with a low-density polar funnel ($ρ\propto r^{-2}$; half-opening angle $\approx15^\circ$). Applying an analytic jet stability model to the simulated envelope, we find that luminous ULGRBs operate their jets near the stability threshold. Thus, many ULGRB jets are too weak to break out and perish inside their envelopes, implying the existence of a class of low-luminosity ULGRBs powered by failed jets. Powerful ($L_{\rm jet}\gtrsim{\rm few}\times10^{47}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$), ultra-relativistic ($γ_{\rm j}\sim100$), narrowly collimated ($θ_{\rm b}\simeq 1^\circ$) jets can survive the current-driven kink instability, escape, and reproduce the observed high isotropic-equivalent luminosity of $\sim10^{51}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$. After breakout, jet widening ($θ_{\rm b}\propto t$), combined with wind-suppressed accretion ($L_{\rm jet}\propto t^{-2}$), produces the steep early X-ray decline ($L_{\rm X,iso}\propto t^{-4}$); once the jet widens to the scale of the funnel walls, its opening angle saturates at $\simeq 10^\circ$, and the decline returns to the intrinsic $t^{-2}$. Together, our simulations and jet stability constraints favor narrow, highly relativistic jets as the engines of luminous ULGRBs and predict early jet breaks, motivating early multi-wavelength follow-up of future events.
